video.title: Could this really work in Korea? A complete roundup of the 4.5-day workweek debate [We Rounded It Up] / SBS News

agents.title: Take a Whole Weekday Off
agents.subtitle: Fewer commutes, more usable time
agents.stance: Adopt a four- or four-and-a-half-day week, preferably with a full weekday off. Commenters disagree on phasing, pay, and total hours.
agents.reasoning: Commenters say a full day off saves a commute and makes time for family and errands. Some expect cutting unnecessary meetings and reports to help maintain output.
agents.full_stance: The position is that a four-day or four-and-a-half-day workweek should be introduced to give people more time outside work. One particularly prominent view is that having an entire weekday off is better than leaving work a little earlier each day. Opinions differ, however, on whether to start with a four-and-a-half-day week and how to handle pay and total weekly hours.

arguments.text: Cutting one workday would save commuting time and transportation costs. The benefit of leaving early can be hard to feel when overtime gets in the way, and even a half day still means going in, so taking the whole day off is seen as the better option.

Having an uninterrupted block of time on a weekday could let people spend time with family, help with household chores, go to medical appointments or run errands at government offices, or work on personal development.

The hope is that by cutting unnecessary meetings, reporting, and waiting time and focusing on the remaining workdays, people could maintain their output while working fewer hours or become more productive per hour.

Recalling that the five-day workweek also faced pushback at first but eventually became the norm, some argue that rather than putting the change off over concerns alone, it should be tried and adjusted if problems arise.
There is some hope that more leisure time could lead people to go out and spend more, and that companies might hire additional workers to cover gaps left by the shorter workweek.

variations.text: Some would take more time off even if it meant lower pay, while others would accept only a small pay cut. Still others support the change only if their current pay is maintained.

Some propose squeezing the workweek into four days, even if that means longer workdays, to get a whole day off. Others propose switching to a four-day week and also cutting the hours worked on those days.

Some favor moving straight to a four-day workweek, some prefer a four-and-a-half-day week to leaving early every day, and others want to start with a four-and-a-half-day week before moving to four days. There are also proposals to have a four-day workweek every other week or to schedule half days on different days for different employees.

Some call for introducing the change across the board rather than starting with public employees alone, while others think businesses will follow if government offices and banks go first. Some say hospital and service workers should also get more time off, while others want government offices and banks exempted for the convenience of the people who use them. Some replies say they would accept the inconvenience even if getting deliveries or shopping at supermarkets became harder.

Some argue that the change should be mandated by law to ensure people actually get the day off. Others favor making a shorter workweek the default while giving people who want to work more that option. There is also concern that cutting hours without reducing workloads could make work more intense.

limitations: Brief comments expressing support or urging a quick rollout do not tell us what work schedule or pay conditions the commenters prefer.

Recollections of how the five-day workweek became the norm, accounts of working shorter hours, and views about effects on productivity, spending, and employment reflect the experiences and expectations expressed in the comments. This material alone cannot establish the actual effects or whether the change would be feasible in different industries.

Before I tried it, I was like, ugh, how am I supposed to work that long in one day? 😭 (9.5 hours, not counting breaks.) But once I actually did it, I liked working my butt off for four days and getting three days off every week better...

agents.title: Shorten Each Workday Instead
agents.subtitle: More time every weekday
agents.stance: Keep five workdays but shorten them; some commenters prioritize flexible start and finish times even if total hours stay the same.
agents.reasoning: Commenters say earlier finishes help with childcare and family dinners while preserving daily workflow. They argue that a half-day Friday gains little if other workdays get longer.
agents.full_stance: The prevailing view is that rather than getting more time off through a four-day or four-and-a-half-day workweek, it would be better to shorten the workday and free up time every weekday, even if the five-day week stays in place. Some also say it is more important to let people adjust their own start and finish times than to have everyone leave at the same time.

arguments.text: Leaving work an hour or two earlier every day would give people time to have dinner with their families, pick up their children, exercise, or read. The idea is that what would really change daily life is having time to use every weekday rather than getting it all on one particular day.

Critics say that working longer Monday through Thursday to make Friday a half day does not reduce total working hours and only cuts into free time on the other weekdays. What matters is whether people actually work fewer hours, not what the policy is called.

Some think that if there are tasks to handle every weekday, keeping the same number of workdays makes it easier to keep work flowing. One commenter recounted how a team took annual leave on top of a four-and-a-half-day schedule, bringing the next team's work to a halt. Others expect people to concentrate better if they spend less time staying late with nothing to do.

Even without cutting working hours, flexible start and finish times would let people plan their days around errands or caregiving. One commenter found that starting and finishing early helped balance morning and afternoon work. Another suggested that parents could stagger their start times so one could handle school drop-off and the other could take care of the children in the afternoon.

Some suggest giving people more annual leave and letting them take it without feeling judged, rather than changing everyone's weekly schedule. Another suggestion is that people whose jobs can be done from home could get back the time they spend commuting, even if they still work the same number of days.

variations.text: Some say working from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. would be enough, while others say they would not feel the difference unless they could leave around 4 p.m. Some replies favor working from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., but others scoff at cutting hours by that much and suggest starting at 8 a.m. and taking a short lunch break instead.

Some propose shortening or skipping lunch and other breaks to get home earlier, while others propose counting lunch as paid work time. Some would actually rather extend lunch to two hours and still leave at 5 p.m.

Not everyone opposes a four-and-a-half-day workweek. Some would prefer shorter days as long as there is no overtime but would still welcome a four-and-a-half-day week. One commenter liked how leaving early on Friday made the weekend feel longer but found that it interrupted the flow of work. Others say that if their jobs make it hard to leave early every day, they would take a pay cut just to have Friday afternoons off.

Views also differ on how these arrangements should be put into practice. Some suggest scheduling around each industry's service hours or staggering days off to avoid gaps in weekday coverage. Others say remote work should be introduced only once network security is assured. There are also calls to stop work-related messages and calls after hours, in addition to letting people leave earlier.

Those who say pay cuts should be prevented worry that people could end up taking on side jobs to make up for lost income. Others say they would choose more time even at lower pay if they could work remotely, hold another job, and work hours that match their actual workload.

limitations: Comments that simply give a preferred finish time or express agreement do not reveal the reasons behind those views or what conditions the commenters would set regarding pay or overtime.

Work delays, better concentration, and lighter caregiving burdens are things commenters either experienced or expect. These comments alone cannot establish how the policy would affect different industries or whether it would be feasible.

agents.title: Fix Unpaid Overtime First
agents.subtitle: Enforce existing hours and leave
agents.stance: Before shortening the week, reform bundled overtime pay and enforce five-day schedules, on-time finishes, holidays, and annual leave. Views on shortening differ.
agents.reasoning: Commenters argue that overtime pay should reflect actual hours and warn that without workload or staffing changes, shorter schedules could push work into evenings and weekends.
agents.full_stance: The position is that before introducing a four-day or four-and-a-half-day workweek, the all-inclusive wage system should be reformed so that people are paid for the overtime and holiday work they actually do, and that a five-day workweek, leaving on time, days off, and annual leave should be guaranteed in practice. Opinions differ on shortening the workweek itself, but there is a shared concern that if unpaid overtime and weekend work continue as they are, only the schedule on paper will change.

arguments.text: The all-inclusive wage system is seen as an excuse for not properly paying people for the overtime and holiday work they actually do. The argument is that companies should do more than just record when people clock in and out: they should pay for the overtime actually worked. Only then will they have an incentive to cut back on overtime.

Citing experiences of six-day workweeks, having to come in on weekends and holidays, and employers ignoring both the 52-hour weekly limit and scheduled end times, some say the existing rules should be enforced before new ones are made. Some also point to cases where a job is advertised as five days a week but the actual contract requires six, leaving workers to use annual leave just to get a day off. They call for guarantees of days off and annual leave, as well as investigations into actual working conditions and enforcement of the rules.

Some expect that if the number of workdays is cut without changing workloads or staffing, the leftover work will spill over into weekday overtime, extra weekend shifts, or work done from home after hours. They suggest adjusting schedules and redistributing work or hiring more staff to actually reduce working hours.

variations.text: Some call for abolishing or banning the all-inclusive wage system outright, while others propose excluding office jobs and clearly specifying which industries and roles can still use it. Some also distinguish between jobs where overtime pay is bundled into wages but workers are guaranteed to leave on time and jobs where workers are made to work unlimited overtime.

Some want overtime banned altogether, while others say work could just move to people's homes or cafés even if the office closes, so it would be better to pay separately for overtime that is hard to avoid. Some commenters say they would rather be paid separately for the overtime they actually work, even if it means a lower base monthly salary.

Some favor improving basic working conditions before moving to a four-day workweek or letting people leave early on Fridays, while others support further cuts in working hours as long as pay and productivity are maintained. Still others favor abolishing the all-inclusive wage system, seeing what happens, and avoiding a blanket rollout. Some say they would rather leave at the scheduled time and get their evenings back every day than have more days off.

Some commenters quip that only a few companies will reap the benefits while people already working six days a week will carry on as before. Others say that even if shorter hours are up for discussion, the first questions should be how to protect hourly workers' incomes and whether demanding the same output in less time on factory floors would make the work more intense and increase the risk of accidents.

limitations: Some comments simply call for abolishing the all-inclusive wage system or guaranteeing a five-day workweek, so it is unclear whether those commenters would support a four-and-a-half-day workweek once those measures were in place.

The long working hours, unpaid extra work, and limits on taking leave are experiences and claims shared in the comments. This material alone cannot establish what conditions are like across entire industries or what effects reforms would have on overtime, hiring, or safety.

representative_comments.text: We should abolish the all-inclusive wage system before moving to a four-day workweek.
representative_comments.original_text: 주 4일보다 포괄 임금제를 먼저 없애야 합니다.

representative_comments.text:
First, it’s not an issue for salaried workers, but what about hourly workers? Almost everyone working in factories run by small and midsize businesses is paid by the hour, and they’re already scraping by on what they make each month. If you cut the number of days they work, how are you going to make up for the pay they lose?

Second, whether it’s 4.5 days, 4 days, or hell, even 3 days, it’s pointless as long as the all-inclusive wage system is in place. Fix that first.

Third, the 52-hour workweek isn’t even being properly enforced yet, and you want to introduce a 4.5-day workweek? Enforce the 52-hour workweek properly first.

Fourth, for people working on the shop floor, especially in factories, do you really think factories will cut production just because working hours are shorter? No. Absolutely not. Never. They’ll raise the hourly production quota to make up for it. If workers have to rush to meet higher quotas in less time, workplace accidents could become more frequent, and the work will get more intense too. How are you going to take responsibility for that?

This isn’t the kind of bullshit we heard about how a five-day workweek would ruin the country. I’m being realistic here. Outside of big corporations and state-owned enterprises, most businesses in this country are small or midsize, and they don’t even have the basics in place yet.

Whether it’s a 4.5-day or a 4-day workweek isn’t the point. Get the groundwork in place first, then talk about it. Isn’t it too early to just barrel ahead and implement it? Do things in order. Trying to cram it all in at once seems like too much.

agents.title: Keep Services Open
agents.subtitle: Coverage plans tailored to each sector
agents.stance: Views on shorter weeks differ, but commenters want sector-specific coverage plans that distinguish employees’ days off from operating days.
agents.reasoning: Commenters warn that shared days off could close banks, clinics, and public offices when people need them. Staggered shifts may help, but staffing remains a concern.
agents.full_stance: The idea is that rather than putting every workplace on the same four-day or four-and-a-half-day schedule, employees’ workdays should be kept separate from the days their workplaces are open, and each industry should first work out how to prevent gaps in service. Opinions are divided on shortening the workweek itself, but one point stands out: if banks, hospitals, and government offices all close on the same day, the benefit of being able to run errands more easily on a weekday may disappear.

arguments.text: If people have the same days off as banks, hospitals, and government offices, they’ll still have to use a half-day or a day of annual leave to run errands. The point is that a convenience people enjoy when only some companies shorten their workweeks can’t automatically be counted as a benefit of a nationwide rollout. It’s also unfair to assume that service workers alone will keep working their usual schedules.

Some worry that if workplaces are actually open fewer days, the effects could go beyond personal errands: gaps in care, delivery delays, longer waits for consultations, and limited access to transportation and logistics services. Some comments exaggerate what it would be like if everything shut down at once, poking fun at people who expect services to run as usual even on their own days off.

One counterargument is that employees could take different days or half-days off and work in rotation, shortening each person’s workweek while keeping the workplace open on weekdays. Others respond that if staffing stays the same and work piles up on certain days, the employees on duty could face heavier workloads and customers could have longer waits.

Some argue that workplaces where staff need to be on site or work in shifts, such as those in manufacturing, construction, and healthcare, can’t easily adopt the same schedules as office workers. Reorganizing shifts and hiring more staff are suggested as alternatives, but labor costs and difficulty finding workers could make these changes hard to carry out, especially for small businesses.

Rather than rolling it out nationwide all at once, some suggest letting workplaces that can manage it adopt it voluntarily or piloting it at a few sites before deciding whether to expand it. Other proposals include offering incentives to participating companies or letting industries that would struggle to make the change keep their current schedules.

variations.text: Some people don’t oppose a shorter workweek and welcome having more time for themselves and their families. They just don’t buy the argument that it would make it easier to visit banks or government offices on weekdays. Other commenters oppose the policy because it could mean shorter opening hours.

Opinions are divided on how to handle the public sector. Some suggest keeping government offices on a five-day week; others suggest starting with public institutions and expanding to the private sector. Another suggestion is to stagger days off so that public-sector employees and workers elsewhere have different days off.

While some say to start wherever it’s feasible, others argue it would be unfair if only some office workers benefited or if shift and weekend workers were left working the same schedules as before. Suggestions include laying out a concrete plan for shift workers first or giving people who work Fridays extra pay and a different day off.

In response to concerns that parents would have nowhere to leave their children if schools and childcare facilities closed, one reply says there would be no childcare gap if parents had those same days off.

One counterargument is that neighborhood clinics are independent businesses whose income depends on how much they’re open, so they won’t cut the number of days they see patients. Others point out that even if the doctor who owns the clinic keeps it open, the work schedules of the clinic’s employees are a separate question.

limitations: The comments discuss both four-day and four-and-a-half-day workweeks, and some don’t distinguish between everyone taking the same day off and staggering days off. The comments alone therefore don’t establish which proposal each concern applies to.
Many comments are brief rhetorical questions or sarcastic remarks, so criticism of the claim that services would be easier to access can’t be taken as opposition to the policy as a whole.

Service delays, the possibility of additional hiring, and whether some industries would be exempt are predictions or claims raised in the comments, not evidence of what actually happened after implementation or of which workplaces the policy has been confirmed to cover.

representative_comments.text:
What's even funnier is that people here assume government offices, banks, and hospitals won't take the same days off as them. Sure, let's say private clinics are independent businesses and can set their own hours, like taking Sundays and Mondays off. But do you really think government offices and banks will change which days they're closed? Hahaha.
What kind of mindset is it to want Friday, Saturday, and Sunday off for yourself but expect everyone else to take Saturday, Sunday, and Monday off? Even places like testing labs at university hospitals will take the same days off.
Inpatient wards will still run, sure, but the rest of the regular staff will get an extra weekend day. That means longer waits at hospitals. Government offices will make the switch first. Civil servants are always the first to try out this kind of thing. Taking turns working 4.5 days doesn't make sense either. The workload is the same every day, but then one person ends up doing two or three times the work...?? And some people would get Friday, Saturday, and Sunday off, while others would have to take Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday off. Who's going to go for that? I'm not against the 4.5-day workweek itself. I just think it's funny that people think it'll let them take care of the bank and government office errands they've been putting off.

representative_comments.text: 12:40 If a four-day workweek is rolled out in full, wouldn't government offices be the first to adopt it? And banks too... Having more time for yourself and your family is great, but I think the reason people say it makes it easier to get things done at government offices and banks is that only some companies have adopted it so far. agents.title: Test the Economics First
agents.subtitle: Pay, jobs, and output
agents.stance: Defer or reject a four-and-a-half-day week unless output, jobs, and pay are addressed. Some accept pay adjustments; others reject income cuts.
agents.reasoning: Commenters say productivity gains aren’t automatic. They warn that maintaining salaries could raise costs and curb hiring, while fewer paid hours could hurt hourly workers.
agents.full_stance: The prevailing position is to oppose a 4.5-day workweek or hold off on introducing it. Shorter hours do not automatically raise hourly productivity, so the view is that the first questions should be whether current output can be maintained, who would bear the cost if wages stay the same, and how workers would make ends meet if wages fall. Those calling for wage adjustments, however, propose a different solution from those who would rather keep current hours than take a pay cut.

arguments.text: The argument is that shorter working hours are a result of higher productivity, not a guarantee that the same output can be achieved in less time. In manufacturing in particular, where output is tied to how long equipment runs, it could become harder to meet production targets and delivery deadlines, weakening export competitiveness. On this view, improving efficiency or changing the structure of industry should come first.

The view is that cutting working hours while keeping monthly pay unchanged would raise labor costs per hour. There are concerns that businesses with little room to absorb the cost could close or cut staff, while others might hire fewer entry-level workers in favor of experienced ones or invest in automation instead of hiring people.

The cost of keeping wages unchanged would not disappear; it could simply shift elsewhere. If companies raise prices, workers could lose purchasing power even if their pay stays the same. If the government subsidizes companies or workers, the question remains where the money would come from.

Designing the policy around monthly salaries alone could overlook income losses for people who rely on hourly or daily pay, overtime pay, or extra-shift premiums. If workers have to make up the lost income with a side job, the extra time off will not translate into rest. Some therefore prioritize the chance to work and earn over more time off.

variations.text: Views differ on whether to adjust wages. Some favor cutting monthly pay in proportion to the reduction in hours while preserving the option to work more and earn more. Others see no reason to shorten hours if it means taking a pay cut. One proposed compromise is to give smaller salary increases in the future rather than cut pay now.

Some are in favor under certain conditions. One view is that the policy should be introduced if labor costs can be reduced or the current workload can be maintained under a performance-based system, with more flexibility to dismiss underperforming employees. Others would base wage adjustments on company performance rather than dismissal conditions, adjusting pay only if performance declines. There is also a view that even a three-day workweek would be acceptable if productivity holds up.

Instead of a blanket rollout, some propose letting companies adopt the policy voluntarily if they can maintain output, or letting only those who want more time off opt in even if it means earning less. Others say leaving work at 5 p.m. every day is more realistic than a four-day workweek.

Unlike those who expect employment to fall, some think reducing pay in proportion to the cut in hours could free up money to hire more workers, or that employers could bring in new staff so employees can rotate shifts.

Some oppose using tax revenue to make up for lost wages. Others think the policy could only be introduced with government support or propose tax breaks for companies that voluntarily adopt it while maintaining output.

limitations: The points about output, hiring, prices, and public finances are predictions and claims made by commenters. This material alone cannot establish the actual effects or causal relationships in examples from other countries.

The comments sometimes discuss four-day and 4.5-day workweeks, reductions in total working hours, rearrangements of workdays, and even abolishing the system that bundles overtime pay into a fixed salary. Not all concerns assume the same policy design.

Some brief comments only express concern about pay cuts or difficulty finding a job. Those concerns alone do not establish whether the commenters ultimately support or oppose the policy, or which alternative they prefer.

representative_comments.text:
Average working hours go down when output per hour rises enough that there's no longer any need to work longer.

The point is that productivity doesn't go up just because the state, political hacks, or bureaucrats change the laws, rewrite the rules, and force people to comply.

The government itself is nothing more than a cost center that produces nothing. Is it even remotely plausible that it can raise companies' productivity by changing the law?

Do these people even know what productivity is?

Shorter working hours are a result of higher productivity. It doesn't work the other way around. By that logic, if the government mandated a one-day workweek, would the government or the president have instantly raised productivity fivefold? Of course not.
